items.stem: The statement above was most likely prompted by which of the following world events?
items.stimulus: “Whereas the laws and treaties of the United States, without interfering with the free expression of opinion and sympathy, or with the commercial manufacture or sale of arms or munitions of war, nevertheless impose upon all persons who may be within their territory and jurisdiction the duty of an impartial neutrality during the existence of the contest; And Whereas it is the duty of a neutral government not to permit or suffer the making of its waters subservient to the purposes of war…. “Now, Therefore, I, Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States of America, in order to preserve the neutrality of the United States…do hereby declare and proclaim…. “That the statutes and the treaties of the United States and the law of nations alike require that no person, within the territory and jurisdiction of the United States, shall take part, directly or indirectly, in the said wars, but shall remain at peace with all of the said belligerents, and shall maintain a strict and impartial neutrality….” Source: Woodrow Wilson, 1914
options: Cuban revolt against Spanish control
Adolph Hitler’s invasion of Poland
Austria-Hungary declaring war on Serbia
Mussolini’s invasion of Ethiopia
items.explanation: Since 1914 was the beginning of World War I, only (C) is relevant. All the other answers represent conflicts in different eras.

option_explanations.A: The Cuban revolt against Spain (1895-98) belongs to the Spanish-American War era, not to Wilson's 1914 neutrality proclamation.
option_explanations.B: Hitler's invasion of Poland (1939) began World War II — a generation after Wilson's 1914 proclamation.
option_explanations.C: Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia in July 1914 ignited World War I. Wilson's neutrality proclamation of August 1914 was the direct American response.
option_explanations.D: Mussolini's invasion of Ethiopia (1935) came two decades later, in the run-up to World War II.

items.stem: All of the following helped contribute to a reversal in the policy described above EXCEPT
items.stimulus: “Whereas the laws and treaties of the United States, without interfering with the free expression of opinion and sympathy, or with the commercial manufacture or sale of arms or munitions of war, nevertheless impose upon all persons who may be within their territory and jurisdiction the duty of an impartial neutrality during the existence of the contest; And Whereas it is the duty of a neutral government not to permit or suffer the making of its waters subservient to the purposes of war…. “Now, Therefore, I, Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States of America, in order to preserve the neutrality of the United States…do hereby declare and proclaim…. “That the statutes and the treaties of the United States and the law of nations alike require that no person, within the territory and jurisdiction of the United States, shall take part, directly or indirectly, in the said wars, but shall remain at peace with all of the said belligerents, and shall maintain a strict and impartial neutrality….” Source: Woodrow Wilson, 1914
options: pressure from large contingents of American Irish and German immigrants
unrestricted German naval attacks on American merchant ships
efforts by the Central Powers to enlist support from American neighbor states
the exit of Czarist Russia from the war
items.explanation: This question is effectively asking us about causes of America entering World War I. America was opposed to German naval attacks on its ships. Eliminate (B). Germany tried to enlist support from Mexico against the United States with the Zimmerman telegram, so eliminate (C). The exit of Czarist Russia allowed Wilson to press the case for intervention more easily, since the Allies could now be cast as democracies fighting autocracy, removing (D). Choice (A) is the best answer because Irish and German immigrants were the most resistant to America joining the war, preferring that the country not openly support the British side.

option_explanations.A: Irish and German Americans were the groups most resistant to entering the war against Germany. Their pressure worked to preserve neutrality, not to reverse it — this is the exception.
option_explanations.B: Unrestricted German submarine attacks on American merchant ships genuinely pushed the U.S. toward war, so this is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Germany's attempt to enlist Mexico against the U.S. (the Zimmermann telegram) genuinely pushed the U.S. toward war, so this is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Czarist Russia's exit from the war let Wilson frame the conflict as democracy versus autocracy, easing his case for intervention — so this is not the exception.

items.stem: Which of the following is true of an effect of the change in America’s war policy referenced above after 1917?
items.stimulus: “Whereas the laws and treaties of the United States, without interfering with the free expression of opinion and sympathy, or with the commercial manufacture or sale of arms or munitions of war, nevertheless impose upon all persons who may be within their territory and jurisdiction the duty of an impartial neutrality during the existence of the contest; And Whereas it is the duty of a neutral government not to permit or suffer the making of its waters subservient to the purposes of war…. “Now, Therefore, I, Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States of America, in order to preserve the neutrality of the United States…do hereby declare and proclaim…. “That the statutes and the treaties of the United States and the law of nations alike require that no person, within the territory and jurisdiction of the United States, shall take part, directly or indirectly, in the said wars, but shall remain at peace with all of the said belligerents, and shall maintain a strict and impartial neutrality….” Source: Woodrow Wilson, 1914
options: The federal government established permanent systems of wage and price controls in support of the war effort.
Courts invoked the First Amendment to protect critics of the war from imprisonment.
Wartime production led to widespread food shortages after the war.
Government-funded propaganda was used to influence public opinion toward the war.
items.explanation: This question is asking us about effects of Wilson’s decision to go to war later. Though the government did establish systems of wage and price controls, they were not permanent, so eliminate (A). Lawyers invoked the First Amendment to protect critics of the war in cases like Schenck v. United States , but the Supreme Court offered little support for these ideas, so eliminate (B). Rather than food shortages, the United States had an oversupply of crop production after the war, so eliminate (C). Choice (D) is correct because the Creel Committee did exactly this.

option_explanations.A: Wartime wage and price controls were temporary emergency measures, not permanent systems.
option_explanations.B: Courts did not protect war critics. In Schenck v. United States (1919) the Supreme Court upheld convictions for antiwar speech under the 'clear and present danger' test.
option_explanations.C: The United States had crop oversupply, not food shortages, after the war.
option_explanations.D: The Committee on Public Information (the Creel Committee) ran a vast government-funded propaganda campaign — posters, films, 'Four-Minute Men' — to turn public opinion toward the war.

items.stem: The policy invoked above is most similar to American foreign policy immediately prior to
items.stimulus: “Whereas the laws and treaties of the United States, without interfering with the free expression of opinion and sympathy, or with the commercial manufacture or sale of arms or munitions of war, nevertheless impose upon all persons who may be within their territory and jurisdiction the duty of an impartial neutrality during the existence of the contest; And Whereas it is the duty of a neutral government not to permit or suffer the making of its waters subservient to the purposes of war…. “Now, Therefore, I, Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States of America, in order to preserve the neutrality of the United States…do hereby declare and proclaim…. “That the statutes and the treaties of the United States and the law of nations alike require that no person, within the territory and jurisdiction of the United States, shall take part, directly or indirectly, in the said wars, but shall remain at peace with all of the said belligerents, and shall maintain a strict and impartial neutrality….” Source: Woodrow Wilson, 1914
options: the Vietnam War
World War II
the 2003 Iraq War
the Spanish–American War
items.explanation: In this excerpt, Wilson is promising a policy of nonintervention (even if he didn’t stick to that later). Look for an answer choice that is also reflective of that same policy. The United States never promised nonintervention in Vietnam, having spent years funding South Vietnam before it sent its own troops, so eliminate (A). In 2003, America was still reeling from the September 11 attacks and was involved in the War on Terror. For the Spanish-American War, the United States had been itching to gain land from Spain well before the war started, so eliminate (D). Choice (B) is the best answer because the United States passed several neutrality acts before World War II, not entering until Pearl Harbor.

option_explanations.A: The United States never promised nonintervention in Vietnam — it funded South Vietnam for years before sending its own troops.
option_explanations.B: Immediately before World War II the United States again proclaimed neutrality, passing the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s — the same nonintervention posture Wilson announced in 1914.
option_explanations.C: The 2003 Iraq invasion was active American intervention, the opposite of neutrality.
option_explanations.D: Before the Spanish-American War the United States was eager to intervene in Cuba (yellow journalism, the Maine), not committed to neutrality.

items.stem: Which of the following statements is true of America and its involvement in World War I?
items.stimulus: “Whereas the laws and treaties of the United States, without interfering with the free expression of opinion and sympathy, or with the commercial manufacture or sale of arms or munitions of war, nevertheless impose upon all persons who may be within their territory and jurisdiction the duty of an impartial neutrality during the existence of the contest; And Whereas it is the duty of a neutral government not to permit or suffer the making of its waters subservient to the purposes of war…. “Now, Therefore, I, Woodrow Wilson, President of the United States of America, in order to preserve the neutrality of the United States…do hereby declare and proclaim…. “That the statutes and the treaties of the United States and the law of nations alike require that no person, within the territory and jurisdiction of the United States, shall take part, directly or indirectly, in the said wars, but shall remain at peace with all of the said belligerents, and shall maintain a strict and impartial neutrality….” Source: Woodrow Wilson, 1914
options: After World War I, debates intensified over American involvement overseas.
After World War I, Americans generally favored the new era of American involvement overseas.
American involvement in World War I was an extension of a long tradition of involvement overseas.
American involvement in World War I was a direct result of “dollar diplomacy.”
items.explanation: The global ramifications of World War I and wartime patriotism and xenophobia, combined with social tensions created by increased international migration, resulted in a general sentiment of isolationism in America.

option_explanations.A: World War I produced an isolationist backlash and a bitter fight over the League of Nations — debates over America's overseas role intensified after the war.
option_explanations.B: Americans did not generally favor continued overseas involvement; the 1920s turned sharply isolationist.
option_explanations.C: Entering a European great-power war broke with the long tradition of avoiding such entanglements; it was not an extension of it.
option_explanations.D: 'Dollar diplomacy' (Taft's policy) did not cause American entry into World War I.

items.stem: This source is best understood in the context of
items.stimulus: “Since the foundations of the American commonwealth were laid in colonial times over 300 years ago, vigorous complaint and more or less bitter persecution have been aimed at newcomers to our shores. Also the congressional reports of about 1840 are full of abuse of English, Scotch, Welsh immigrants as paupers, criminals, and so forth. Old citizens in Detroit of Irish and German descent have told me of the fierce tirades and propaganda directed against the great waves of Irish and Germans who came over from 1840 on for a few decades to escape civil, racial, and religious persecution in their native lands. The “Know-Nothings,” lineal ancestors of the Ku-Klux Klan, bitterly denounced the Irish and Germans as mongrels, scum, foreigners, and a menace to our institutions, much as other great branches of the Caucasian race of glorious history and antecedents are berated to-day…. But to-day it is the Italians, Spanish, Poles, Jews, Greeks, Russians, Balkanians, and so forth, who are the racial lepers…. In this bill we find racial discrimination at its worst—a deliberate attempt to go back 84 years in our census taken every 10 years so that a blow may be aimed at peoples of eastern and southern Europe, particularly at our recent allies in the Great War—Poland and Italy.” Source: Robert H. Clancy, Congressional Record , 68th Congress, 1st Session, 1924
options: World War I patriotism
immigration quotas
labor strikes
the Red Scare
items.explanation: Clancy is denouncing immigration quotas as “racial discrimination at its worst.” Choice (A) is far too positive for the tone of this excerpt. Choice (C), labor strikes, are not mentioned. Choice (D), the Red Scare, is a tempting choice, but the excerpt does not mention communism specifically. Many of the ethnic groups mentioned are wholly unconnected to communism.

option_explanations.A: The excerpt's tone is bitter denunciation of nativist persecution, not World War I patriotism.
option_explanations.B: Clancy is denouncing the 1920s immigration quota acts as 'racial discrimination at its worst' — the source belongs to the debate over immigration quotas.
option_explanations.C: Labor strikes are never mentioned in the excerpt.
option_explanations.D: Communism is never mentioned. The persecuted groups named (Irish, Germans, and others) are not connected to communism in the passage.

items.stem: What best accounts for the sharp increase of immigrants during the period 1880–1910?
items.stimulus: “Since the foundations of the American commonwealth were laid in colonial times over 300 years ago, vigorous complaint and more or less bitter persecution have been aimed at newcomers to our shores. Also the congressional reports of about 1840 are full of abuse of English, Scotch, Welsh immigrants as paupers, criminals, and so forth. Old citizens in Detroit of Irish and German descent have told me of the fierce tirades and propaganda directed against the great waves of Irish and Germans who came over from 1840 on for a few decades to escape civil, racial, and religious persecution in their native lands. The “Know-Nothings,” lineal ancestors of the Ku-Klux Klan, bitterly denounced the Irish and Germans as mongrels, scum, foreigners, and a menace to our institutions, much as other great branches of the Caucasian race of glorious history and antecedents are berated to-day…. But to-day it is the Italians, Spanish, Poles, Jews, Greeks, Russians, Balkanians, and so forth, who are the racial lepers…. In this bill we find racial discrimination at its worst—a deliberate attempt to go back 84 years in our census taken every 10 years so that a blow may be aimed at peoples of eastern and southern Europe, particularly at our recent allies in the Great War—Poland and Italy.” Source: Robert H. Clancy, Congressional Record , 68th Congress, 1st Session, 1924
options: Many Southern and Eastern Europeans turned to America for financial gain and political freedom.
Irish farmers were forced to leave their homes because of agricultural disasters.
Germans were seeking ways to avoid military conscription.
The United States welcomed immigrants by providing housing and employment.
items.explanation: The largest wave of immigration to this country occurred during this period and was a result of political and economic upheaval. This so-called “new immigration” brought immigrants from Southern and Eastern Europe as well as Asia. Between 1880 and 1910, approximately 12 million people came to the United States, many to escape poverty or political persecution.

option_explanations.A: The 1880-1910 'new immigration' brought Southern and Eastern Europeans (and Asians) fleeing poverty and upheaval, drawn by American jobs and political freedom — some 12 million people.
option_explanations.B: The Irish famine migration was in the 1840s-50s, not the 1880-1910 wave.
option_explanations.C: Avoiding German military conscription was not the driver of the 1880-1910 immigration surge.
option_explanations.D: The United States provided no housing or jobs to immigrants; newcomers faced harsh tenement and sweatshop conditions.

items.stem: The policy criticized above was most challenged by laws associated with which of the following?
items.stimulus: “Since the foundations of the American commonwealth were laid in colonial times over 300 years ago, vigorous complaint and more or less bitter persecution have been aimed at newcomers to our shores. Also the congressional reports of about 1840 are full of abuse of English, Scotch, Welsh immigrants as paupers, criminals, and so forth. Old citizens in Detroit of Irish and German descent have told me of the fierce tirades and propaganda directed against the great waves of Irish and Germans who came over from 1840 on for a few decades to escape civil, racial, and religious persecution in their native lands. The “Know-Nothings,” lineal ancestors of the Ku-Klux Klan, bitterly denounced the Irish and Germans as mongrels, scum, foreigners, and a menace to our institutions, much as other great branches of the Caucasian race of glorious history and antecedents are berated to-day…. But to-day it is the Italians, Spanish, Poles, Jews, Greeks, Russians, Balkanians, and so forth, who are the racial lepers…. In this bill we find racial discrimination at its worst—a deliberate attempt to go back 84 years in our census taken every 10 years so that a blow may be aimed at peoples of eastern and southern Europe, particularly at our recent allies in the Great War—Poland and Italy.” Source: Robert H. Clancy, Congressional Record , 68th Congress, 1st Session, 1924
options: The New Deal
The Great Society
The Contract with America
The Fair Deal
items.explanation: Here, the source is referencing the 1924 immigration quota acts, which means we need an answer that contradicted or upended those laws. The law most associated with changing America’s immigration system was the Hart-Celler Immigration Act of 1965. Since that was passed in the 1960s, (B) is the best answer because it fits with the Great Society.

option_explanations.A: The New Deal (1930s) did not overhaul the immigration quota system.
option_explanations.B: The Hart-Celler Immigration Act (1965), passed in Lyndon Johnson's Great Society era, abolished the national-origins quota system the excerpt attacks.
option_explanations.C: The Contract with America (1994) did not reform immigration quotas.
option_explanations.D: Truman's Fair Deal did not overhaul the quota system.

items.stem: The graph above is consistent with which of the following statements about the era portrayed?
items.stimulus: [Described graph — U.S. unemployment rate, 1929–1941 (public-domain style statistical chart; original artwork not reproduced). Unemployment spikes after the 1929 crash and peaks around 1933 at roughly one-quarter of the workforce. It then generally declines through the mid-1930s, rises again during the 1937–1938 downturn, and remains elevated near the end of the decade; a full recovery coincides with U.S. entry into World War II.]
options: Unemployment rates began to drop with the election of Herbert Hoover in 1933.
Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal programs had eliminated unemployment by 1937.
A full economic recovery did not occur until the U.S. involvement in World War II.
A brief economic recovery in 1937 sparked a sudden increase in U.S. employment.
items.explanation: According to the graph, unemployment generally decreased from 1933 onward, but it did not decrease in 1937, so rule out (B). Hoover was not elected in 1933, nor did his administration successfully decrease unemployment, so rule out (A). Be careful with (D)—unemployment increased in 1937; therefore, employment decreased . Since the United States entered World War II in the early 1940s, (C) is a reasonable inference.

option_explanations.A: Hoover was not elected in 1933 — Franklin Roosevelt was. And unemployment did not begin dropping under Hoover.
option_explanations.B: The New Deal reduced unemployment but had not eliminated it by 1937 — it stood near 14% and then rose again in the 1937-38 downturn.
option_explanations.C: The graph shows unemployment peaking around 1933 at roughly a quarter of the workforce, declining unevenly through the 1930s, spiking again in 1937-38, and remaining elevated — full recovery coincides only with U.S. entry into World War II.
option_explanations.D: 1937 brought rising unemployment (the 'Roosevelt recession'), not a sudden employment surge.

items.stem: Which of the following was NOT a major contribution factor to the historical situation shown above before 1930?
items.stimulus: [Described graph — U.S. unemployment rate, 1929–1941 (public-domain style statistical chart; original artwork not reproduced). Unemployment spikes after the 1929 crash and peaks around 1933 at roughly one-quarter of the workforce. It then generally declines through the mid-1930s, rises again during the 1937–1938 downturn, and remains elevated near the end of the decade; a full recovery coincides with U.S. entry into World War II.]
options: Technological advances had allowed farmers and manufacturers to overproduce, creating large inventories.
The federal government interfered too frequently with the economy, causing investors to lose confidence.
Stock investors had been allowed to speculate wildly, creating an unstable and volatile stock market.
Major businesses were controlled by so few producers that the failure of any one had a considerable effect on the national economy.
items.explanation: In fact, the federal government did almost nothing to regulate the economy even though many within the government foresaw the potential for economic disaster. Many possible remedies—an income tax to redistribute wealth, a tighter money supply to discourage speculation, aggressive enforcement of antitrust regulations—were rejected. Meanwhile, manufacturers were overproducing, causing them to stockpile large inventories and lay off workers; consumers weren’t making enough money to buy what, in some cases, they built at work; and the wealth of the nation was concentrated in very few, often irresponsible, hands. The system was too fragile, and when it started to tumble, it fell entirely to pieces very quickly.

option_explanations.A: Overproduction was a genuine pre-1930 cause: technology let farmers and manufacturers produce more than consumers could buy, creating gluts and layoffs — not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The 1920s federal government practiced laissez-faire and did almost nothing to regulate the economy, rejecting remedies like tighter money or antitrust enforcement. 'Too frequent interference' is false — this is the exception.
option_explanations.C: Wild speculation — stocks bought on margin far above underlying values — was a genuine cause of the crash, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Extreme concentration was a genuine cause: when a few giant firms dominated industries, one's failure shook the whole economy — not the exception.

items.stem: The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 sought to lessen the effects of the Depression by
items.stimulus: [Described graph — U.S. unemployment rate, 1929–1941 (public-domain style statistical chart; original artwork not reproduced). Unemployment spikes after the 1929 crash and peaks around 1933 at roughly one-quarter of the workforce. It then generally declines through the mid-1930s, rises again during the 1937–1938 downturn, and remains elevated near the end of the decade; a full recovery coincides with U.S. entry into World War II.]
options: paying farmers to cut production and, in some cases, destroy crops
purchasing farms and turning them into government collectives
instituting an early retirement program for farmers over the age of 50
encouraging farmers to increase production
items.explanation: As he began his first term, Roosevelt was faced with an agricultural market in which the bottom had dropped out; farmers had so overproduced that their crops were worth virtually nothing. Roosevelt’s solution, the Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA), provided payments to farmers in return for their agreement to cut production by up to one-half. The money to cover this program came from increased taxes on meat packers, millers, and other food processors. The program stabilized agricultural prices and increased American farm income, but it came to an end when the Supreme Court declared it unconstitutional in 1936. A second AAA in 1938 served much the same purpose while avoiding those aspects that voided the first AAA.

option_explanations.A: The Agricultural Adjustment Act (1933) paid farmers to cut production by up to half — plowing under crops and destroying surplus livestock — to raise farm prices from rock bottom.
option_explanations.B: The United States did not create government collective farms; that was the Soviet model, not the AAA.
option_explanations.C: There was no early-retirement program for farmers over 50.
option_explanations.D: The AAA did the opposite of encouraging production: it paid farmers to produce less.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would likely be most supportive of policies created in response to the situation depicted above after 1933?
items.stimulus: [Described graph — U.S. unemployment rate, 1929–1941 (public-domain style statistical chart; original artwork not reproduced). Unemployment spikes after the 1929 crash and peaks around 1933 at roughly one-quarter of the workforce. It then generally declines through the mid-1930s, rises again during the 1937–1938 downturn, and remains elevated near the end of the decade; a full recovery coincides with U.S. entry into World War II.]
options: Industrial business owners
African American agricultural workers
Critics of American involvement in European affairs
Labor union organizers
items.explanation: This question is asking about who would have been most supportive of the New Deal policies of FDR. Business owners were probably the single group most critical of the New Deal because of America’s turn away from laissez-faire economics of the 1920s, so eliminate (A). FDR’s policies like social security did little to benefit groups like African American sharecroppers, who were largely excluded from social security’s benefits, so eliminate (B). Roosevelt was pilloried by isolationists like Charles Lindbergh for his veiled support of Great Britain as World War II began, so eliminate (C). Choice (D) is the best answer because the Wagner Act guaranteed the right for unions to collectively bargain, a huge victory for the movement.

option_explanations.A: Industrial business owners were the New Deal's sharpest critics, denouncing its abandonment of 1920s laissez-faire — not its supporters.
option_explanations.B: African American agricultural workers were largely excluded from early New Deal benefits (farm and domestic workers were left out of Social Security) — not its leading supporters.
option_explanations.C: Critics of involvement in European affairs (isolationists) attacked Roosevelt's foreign policy, not the domestic programs in question.
option_explanations.D: Labor union organizers were the New Deal's natural allies: the Wagner Act (1935) protected collective bargaining, and the administration's pro-union stance made organizers its most supportive constituency.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a legal outcome between the president and Supreme Court in the time period referenced above?
items.stimulus: [Described graph — U.S. unemployment rate, 1929–1941 (public-domain style statistical chart; original artwork not reproduced). Unemployment spikes after the 1929 crash and peaks around 1933 at roughly one-quarter of the workforce. It then generally declines through the mid-1930s, rises again during the 1937–1938 downturn, and remains elevated near the end of the decade; a full recovery coincides with U.S. entry into World War II.]
options: Franklin Roosevelt urged the voting public to write letters of protest to Supreme Court justices.
Congress submitted four constitutional amendments broadening the powers of the presidency.
The New Deal was largely abandoned and replaced with laissez-faire economic policy.
The President proposed legislation that would allow him to appoint new federal and Supreme Court judges.
items.explanation: The question refers to Roosevelt’s notorious “court-packing” plan. Unhappy with the Supreme Court and the federal judiciary, whose conservatism frequently resulted in the nullification of New Deal programs, Roosevelt proposed that he be allowed to name a new federal judge for every sitting judge who had reached the age of 70 and not retired. The plan would have allowed Roosevelt to add six new Supreme Court justices and more than 40 other federal judges. The proposal was not at all popular and was roundly defeated in the Senate. It also helped fuel the arguments of those who contended that FDR had grown too powerful. Not long after the “court-packing” incident, several conservative justices retired and FDR replaced them with liberals, so he achieved his goal despite the failure of his plan.

option_explanations.A: Roosevelt did not urge the public to write protest letters to the justices.
option_explanations.B: Congress did not submit constitutional amendments broadening presidential power.
option_explanations.C: The New Deal was not abandoned for laissez-faire; Roosevelt fought to preserve it.
option_explanations.D: Roosevelt's 1937 'court-packing' plan proposed letting him appoint a new federal judge for every sitting judge over 70 who would not retire — up to six new Supreme Court justices — to overcome the conservative Court's nullification of New Deal laws.

items.stem: The conflict described above is most likely a result of which of the following doctrines?
items.stimulus: “We found that not only was it a civil war, an effort by a people who had for years been seeking their liberation from any colonial influence whatsoever, but also we found that the Vietnamese whom we had enthusiastically molded after our own image were hard put to take up the fight against the threat we were supposedly saving them from. “We found most people didn’t even know the difference between communism and democracy. They only wanted to work in rice paddies without helicopters strafing them and bombs with napalm burning their villages and tearing their country apart. They wanted everything to do with the war, particularly with this foreign presence of the United States of America, to leave them alone in peace, and they practiced the art of survival by siding with whichever military force was present at a particular time, be it Viet Cong, North Vietnamese or American.” Source: Statement by John Kerry of Vietnam Veterans Against the War
options: Imperialism
Containment
“Big-stick” diplomacy
Isolationism
items.explanation: The conflict in Vietnam was an attempt to contain the spread of communism in Southeast Asia. It was not an attempt to control the Vietnamese government over the long-term, so rule out (A). Choice (C), “big-stick” diplomacy, may involve the threat of force, but it does not necessarily lead to war. Choice (D), isolationism, would have prevented American involvement in Vietnam.

option_explanations.A: Vietnam was not imperialism in the colonial-control sense; the U.S. aim was not long-term governance of Vietnam but stopping communism's spread.
option_explanations.B: The Vietnam War was containment applied to Southeast Asia — American intervention to prevent communist expansion under the domino theory.
option_explanations.C: 'Big-stick' diplomacy (Theodore Roosevelt's Caribbean policy) relied on the threat of force, but it is not the doctrine behind the Vietnam commitment.
option_explanations.D: Isolationism would have kept America out of Vietnam entirely — the opposite of what happened.

items.stem: The excerpt above can best be used as evidence to prove which of the following historical claims?
items.stimulus: “We found that not only was it a civil war, an effort by a people who had for years been seeking their liberation from any colonial influence whatsoever, but also we found that the Vietnamese whom we had enthusiastically molded after our own image were hard put to take up the fight against the threat we were supposedly saving them from. “We found most people didn’t even know the difference between communism and democracy. They only wanted to work in rice paddies without helicopters strafing them and bombs with napalm burning their villages and tearing their country apart. They wanted everything to do with the war, particularly with this foreign presence of the United States of America, to leave them alone in peace, and they practiced the art of survival by siding with whichever military force was present at a particular time, be it Viet Cong, North Vietnamese or American.” Source: Statement by John Kerry of Vietnam Veterans Against the War
options: By the 1970s, antiwar sentiment had moved beyond a fringe position
Soldiers were more likely to oppose the Vietnam War than civilians.
Prolonged spending on the Vietnam conflict was creating domestic economic challenges.
Republicans owed their electoral success to their Vietnam position.
items.explanation: Consider the claims here and how they relate to the source. It might be true that Richard Nixon became president because he promised to be able to end the Vietnam War, but that has nothing to do with what Kerry is discussing, so eliminate (D). Similarly, the United States was beginning to experience “stagflation” in the 1970s, but that has little bearing on Kerry’s position, so eliminate (C). While it is evident from the source that Kerry is a soldier, you can’t know if his position is indicative of all soldiers, so eliminate (B). Choice (A) is the best answer because the fact that Kerry was invited to speak before Congress indicates that his position is one that has become more acceptable than it was a few years prior.

option_explanations.A: Kerry — a decorated veteran testifying before Congress in 1971 — voices sweeping condemnation of the war. His prominence shows antiwar sentiment had moved from the fringe to the mainstream by the 1970s.
option_explanations.B: The excerpt does not compare soldiers' and civilians' views on the war.
option_explanations.C: Kerry does not discuss the domestic economic effects of war spending.
option_explanations.D: Kerry says nothing about Republicans' electoral fortunes or Nixon's promises.

items.stem: In the 1970s, ideas like those expressed by the author above lent support for which of the following foreign policies?
items.stimulus: “We found that not only was it a civil war, an effort by a people who had for years been seeking their liberation from any colonial influence whatsoever, but also we found that the Vietnamese whom we had enthusiastically molded after our own image were hard put to take up the fight against the threat we were supposedly saving them from. “We found most people didn’t even know the difference between communism and democracy. They only wanted to work in rice paddies without helicopters strafing them and bombs with napalm burning their villages and tearing their country apart. They wanted everything to do with the war, particularly with this foreign presence of the United States of America, to leave them alone in peace, and they practiced the art of survival by siding with whichever military force was present at a particular time, be it Viet Cong, North Vietnamese or American.” Source: Statement by John Kerry of Vietnam Veterans Against the War
options: A more aggressive approach to containing communism in China after the United States left Vietnam
Efforts to build out America’s nuclear arsenal to rely less on costly military interventions
Broad support for anti-communist movements in Latin and South America
Relaxed tensions between the Soviet Union and United States
items.explanation: Choice (C) is true of the 1980s (and doesn’t go well with Kerry’s perspective), so eliminate it. Choice (A) can be eliminated because the United States sought to engage with China more in the 1970s, not contain them. Eisenhower sought to build out America’s nuclear arsenal in the 1950s with the New Look policy, but in the 1970s the United States began signing arms limitations treaties, so eliminate (B). Choice (D) is the best because it describes the policy of “Detente,” which goes well with the sentiments expressed here.

option_explanations.A: In the 1970s the United States moved toward engagement with China (Nixon's 1972 visit), not more aggressive containment of it.
option_explanations.B: The 1970s brought arms-limitation agreements (SALT), not a nuclear buildup to avoid interventions.
option_explanations.C: Broad support for anti-communist movements in Latin America was the 1980s (Reagan), not the 1970s mood Kerry expresses.
option_explanations.D: Kerry's skepticism about military intervention supported detente — the 1970s relaxation of tensions between the United States and the Soviet Union.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would be most likely to support the point of view expressed by Kerry above?
items.stimulus: “We found that not only was it a civil war, an effort by a people who had for years been seeking their liberation from any colonial influence whatsoever, but also we found that the Vietnamese whom we had enthusiastically molded after our own image were hard put to take up the fight against the threat we were supposedly saving them from. “We found most people didn’t even know the difference between communism and democracy. They only wanted to work in rice paddies without helicopters strafing them and bombs with napalm burning their villages and tearing their country apart. They wanted everything to do with the war, particularly with this foreign presence of the United States of America, to leave them alone in peace, and they practiced the art of survival by siding with whichever military force was present at a particular time, be it Viet Cong, North Vietnamese or American.” Source: Statement by John Kerry of Vietnam Veterans Against the War
options: A secretary of state in the 1820s enforcing the Monroe Doctrine
A voter supportive of Manifest Destiny in the 1840s
A journalist writing about the plight of Cubans in the 1890s
A member of the Anti-Imperialist League in the 1900s
items.explanation: In this excerpt, Kerry is expressing skepticism of American military intervention and its ability to be able to effectively spread democracy abroad. Eliminate (A) because supporters of the Monroe Doctrine implicitly believed America had an active role to play in its own hemisphere in terms of foreign policy. Choice (B) can be eliminated because supporters of Manifest Destiny justified war with Mexico on the grounds of spreading American democracy. Choice (C) can be eliminated because Yellow Journalism in the late 1800s encouraged the “Cuba Libre” slogan that justified war with Spain. The Anti-Imperialist League is the best answer because its members shared Kerry’s skepticism of military intervention for humanitarian causes.

option_explanations.A: An 1820s enforcer of the Monroe Doctrine believed America had an active role to play in its hemisphere — the opposite of Kerry's skepticism.
option_explanations.B: An 1840s Manifest Destiny voter justified the Mexican War as spreading American democracy — the opposite of Kerry's doubt that intervention spreads democracy.
option_explanations.C: An 1890s yellow journalist pushed for intervention in Cuba — the opposite of Kerry's anti-intervention stance.
option_explanations.D: The Anti-Imperialist League (founded 1898) opposed overseas empire and doubted that military force could export democracy — the closest match to Kerry's skepticism.

items.stem: From the quote above, it is reasonable to infer that
items.stimulus: “We found that not only was it a civil war, an effort by a people who had for years been seeking their liberation from any colonial influence whatsoever, but also we found that the Vietnamese whom we had enthusiastically molded after our own image were hard put to take up the fight against the threat we were supposedly saving them from. “We found most people didn’t even know the difference between communism and democracy. They only wanted to work in rice paddies without helicopters strafing them and bombs with napalm burning their villages and tearing their country apart. They wanted everything to do with the war, particularly with this foreign presence of the United States of America, to leave them alone in peace, and they practiced the art of survival by siding with whichever military force was present at a particular time, be it Viet Cong, North Vietnamese or American.” Source: Statement by John Kerry of Vietnam Veterans Against the War
options: many Vietnamese viewed the United States as a colonial influence
most Vietnamese were opposed to communism
most Vietnamese favored communism
some Viet Cong fought alongside American troops in opposition to North Vietnam
items.explanation: In the excerpt, Kerry states that the Vietnamese were “a people who had for years been seeking their liberation from any colonial influence whatsoever, ” but they were also “hard put to take up the fight against the threat we were supposedly saving them from.” Thus, it is fair to infer that the Vietnamese did not welcome U.S. involvement in their affairs. Since “most people didn’t even know the difference between communism and democracy,” rule out (B) and (C). Choice (D) is false and unsupported by the excerpt.

option_explanations.A: Kerry describes Vietnamese seeking liberation 'from any colonial influence whatsoever' while resisting the American presence — the fair inference is that many Vietnamese viewed the United States as another colonial power.
option_explanations.B: Kerry explicitly says most Vietnamese 'didn't even know the difference between communism and democracy,' so this cannot be inferred.
option_explanations.C: For the same reason, this cannot be inferred — ideology was not their concern.
option_explanations.D: This is false and unsupported: the Viet Cong fought American troops; they did not fight alongside them.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the relationship between the United States and the Empire of Japan in the years leading up to this speech?
items.stimulus: “Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan. The United States was at peace with that nation and, at the solicitation of Japan, was still in conversation with its Government and its Emperor looking toward the maintenance of peace in the Pacific. Indeed, one hour after Japanese air squadrons had commenced bombing…the Japanese Ambassador to the United States and his colleague delivered to the Secretary of State a formal reply to a recent American message. While this reply stated that it seemed useless to continue the existing diplomatic negotiations, it contained no threat or hint of war or armed attack…. The attack yesterday…has caused severe damage to American naval and military forces. Very many American lives have been lost. In addition American ships have been reported torpedoed on the high seas…. As Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy, I have directed that all measures be taken for our defense.” Source: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, radio address, December 8, 1941
options: Japan and the United States maintained an alliance against Nazi Germany.
The United States and Japan developed tensions over which country rightfully controlled Hawaii.
The United States depended on loans from Japan to stay afloat during the Great Depression.
Japan resented the economic embargoes placed against it by the United States.
items.explanation: Japan’s invasion of China led the United States to place economic sanctions on Japan. Despite negotiations between the two countries to end the embargoes, no satisfactory progress was made and Japan decided to attack the naval base in Hawaii. Choice (D) is correct. Japan held an alliance with Germany, but neither held one with the United States. Eliminate (A). Hawaii was unquestionably United States territory, so (B) is incorrect. While the United States was in a deep recession during the years leading up to the attack on Pearl Harbor, it received no financial aid from Japan. Eliminate (C).

option_explanations.A: Japan was allied with Germany, not with the United States.
option_explanations.B: Hawaii was unquestionably American territory; the two countries had no dispute over who controlled it.
option_explanations.C: The United States did not depend on Japanese loans during the Depression.
option_explanations.D: After Japan invaded China, the United States imposed oil and steel embargoes that strangled Japan's war machine. Despite ongoing negotiations, no settlement was reached, and Japan's resentment of the embargoes led to the decision to strike Pearl Harbor.

items.stem: Which of the following statements best characterizes the economic consequences of the declaration of war described above?
items.stimulus: “Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan. The United States was at peace with that nation and, at the solicitation of Japan, was still in conversation with its Government and its Emperor looking toward the maintenance of peace in the Pacific. Indeed, one hour after Japanese air squadrons had commenced bombing…the Japanese Ambassador to the United States and his colleague delivered to the Secretary of State a formal reply to a recent American message. While this reply stated that it seemed useless to continue the existing diplomatic negotiations, it contained no threat or hint of war or armed attack…. The attack yesterday…has caused severe damage to American naval and military forces. Very many American lives have been lost. In addition American ships have been reported torpedoed on the high seas…. As Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy, I have directed that all measures be taken for our defense.” Source: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, radio address, December 8, 1941
options: Decreased trade with Asian nations precipitated economic recession in both the United States and Europe.
The war-ravaged condition of Asia and Europe allowed the United States to emerge as one of the most prosperous nations on Earth.
Cold War tensions isolated the economies of both the Soviet Union and the United States, leading to economic struggle for both nations.
Japan was subsequently required to pay reparations to the United States, forcing it into a prolonged depression.
items.explanation: There are many red herrings here. You can rule out (A), (C), and (D) by simply remembering that the American economy was very strong after World War II and that Japan was not punished for its actions in the war. In fact, General Douglas MacArthur aided in the rebuilding of Japan, and Japan developed a very strong economy, particularly throughout the 1970s and 1980s.

option_explanations.A: The American economy boomed during and after the war; lost Asian trade caused no recession in the United States or Europe.
option_explanations.B: With Europe and Asia in ruins, the United States — its industry intact and dominant — emerged as one of the most prosperous nations on earth.
option_explanations.C: Cold War tensions did not isolate or impoverish the American economy; the U.S. thrived.
option_explanations.D: Japan was not crushed by reparations. Under MacArthur's occupation it was rebuilt and developed a powerhouse economy, especially in the 1970s and 80s.

items.stem: Which of the following was the most immediate consequence of the events described in the excerpt above?
items.stimulus: “Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan. The United States was at peace with that nation and, at the solicitation of Japan, was still in conversation with its Government and its Emperor looking toward the maintenance of peace in the Pacific. Indeed, one hour after Japanese air squadrons had commenced bombing…the Japanese Ambassador to the United States and his colleague delivered to the Secretary of State a formal reply to a recent American message. While this reply stated that it seemed useless to continue the existing diplomatic negotiations, it contained no threat or hint of war or armed attack…. The attack yesterday…has caused severe damage to American naval and military forces. Very many American lives have been lost. In addition American ships have been reported torpedoed on the high seas…. As Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy, I have directed that all measures be taken for our defense.” Source: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, radio address, December 8, 1941
options: Trade embargoes with Japan extending up through the 1980s
The Battle of Normandy
The internment of Japanese-Americans
The bombing of Nagasaki
items.explanation: Normandy is irrelevant to Japan, so rule out (B). Choice (A) might sound tempting, but it is false; trade relationships with Japan were healthy after World War II. Choice (D) is likewise tempting, but it occurred at the end of World War II. President Truman dropped the bombs, not FDR.

option_explanations.A: U.S.-Japan trade was healthy after World War II; there were no embargoes extending into the 1980s.
option_explanations.B: The Normandy invasion (1944) was in the European theater against Germany — unrelated to Pearl Harbor's aftermath.
option_explanations.C: The most immediate domestic consequence was Executive Order 9066 (February 1942), ordering the internment of more than 110,000 Japanese Americans from the West Coast.
option_explanations.D: Nagasaki was bombed in August 1945, at the war's end — nearly four years later, not the immediate consequence.

items.stem: The above statements were most likely made after which major event?
items.stimulus: “Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan. The United States was at peace with that nation and, at the solicitation of Japan, was still in conversation with its Government and its Emperor looking toward the maintenance of peace in the Pacific. Indeed, one hour after Japanese air squadrons had commenced bombing…the Japanese Ambassador to the United States and his colleague delivered to the Secretary of State a formal reply to a recent American message. While this reply stated that it seemed useless to continue the existing diplomatic negotiations, it contained no threat or hint of war or armed attack…. The attack yesterday…has caused severe damage to American naval and military forces. Very many American lives have been lost. In addition American ships have been reported torpedoed on the high seas…. As Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy, I have directed that all measures be taken for our defense.” Source: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, radio address, December 8, 1941
options: The bombing of Pearl Harbor
The sinking of the U.S.S. Maine
The bombing of the U.S.S. Liberty
The Boxer Rebellion
items.explanation: The date, 1941, places this speech at the beginning of World War II, so only (A) is in the right era.

option_explanations.A: Roosevelt's 'date which will live in infamy' address to Congress on December 8, 1941, followed Japan's December 7 attack on Pearl Harbor — the event the speech describes.
option_explanations.B: The sinking of the USS Maine (1898) triggered the Spanish-American War — the wrong war and the wrong century's end.
option_explanations.C: The USS Liberty incident (1967) occurred during the Six-Day War — decades later.
option_explanations.D: The Boxer Rebellion (1900) was in China — unrelated to a 1941 presidential address.

items.stem: The sentiments expressed in the first excerpt by Abigail Adams best exemplify which of the following ideologies?
items.stimulus: Source 1 “In the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favorable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could. If particular care and attention is not paid to the Ladies we are determined to foment a Rebellion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation.” Source: Abigail Adams, in a letter to John Adams, 1776 Source 2 “Special legislation for woman has placed us in a most anomalous position. Women invested with the rights of citizens in one section—voters, jurors, office-holders—crossing an imaginary line, are subjects in the next. In some States, a married woman may hold property and transact business in her own name; in others, her earnings belong to her husband. In some States, a woman may testify against her husband, sue and be sued in the courts; in others, she has no redress in case of damage to person, property, or character. In case of divorce on account of adultery in the husband, the innocent wife is held to possess no right to children or property, unless by special decree of the court. But in no State of the Union has the wife the right to her own person, or to any part of the joint earnings of the co-partnership during the life of her husband. In some States women may enter the law schools and practice in the courts; in others they are forbidden. In some universities girls enjoy equal educational advantages with boys, while many of the proudest institutions in the land deny them admittance, though the sons of China, Japan and Africa are welcomed there. But the privileges already granted in the several States are by no means secure.” Source: Susan B. Anthony, “Declaration of Rights for Women,” July 4, 1876
options: Second-wave feminism
Jeffersonian democracy
Republican Motherhood
Libertarianism
items.explanation: Abigail Adams, the wife of John Adams, was not a feminist in the strictest sense, but the sentiments in this excerpt do embody the precepts of Republican Motherhood, which called on white women to maintain and teach republican values within the family and granted women a new importance in American political culture. The Adams family was not Jeffersonian Democrat or Libertarian, in the modern sense, so rule out (B) and (D), respectively.

option_explanations.A: Second-wave feminism (1960s-70s) is two centuries after Abigail Adams's 1776 letter.
option_explanations.B: Jeffersonian democracy centered on yeoman farmers and limited government, not on women's role in the family.
option_explanations.C: Abigail Adams's plea embodies Republican Motherhood: the revolutionary-era idea that women, as mothers, would nurture republican virtue in future citizens — giving women new political importance within the family.
option_explanations.D: Libertarianism is a modern anti-statist philosophy, not the ideology of a 1776 appeal for women's legal protections.

items.stem: The sentiments expressed in the second excerpt by Susan

Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could. If particular care and attention is not paid to the Ladies we are determined to foment a Rebellion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation.” Source: Abigail Adams, in a letter to John Adams, 1776 Source 2 “Special legislation for woman has placed us in a most anomalous position. In some States, a married woman may hold property and transact business in her own name; in others, her earnings belong to her husband. In case of divorce on account of adultery in the husband, the innocent wife is held to possess no right to children or property, unless by special decree of the court. But in no State of the Union has the wife the right to her own person, or to any part of the joint earnings of the co-partnership during the life of her husband. In some States women may enter the law schools and practice in the courts; in others they are forbidden. options: the Equal Rights Amendment
universal suffrage
states’ rights
prohibition
items.explanation: 1876 puts this excerpt squarely in the realm of first-wave feminism, which largely campaigned for universal suffrage for all, including women. Choice (A), the Equal Rights Amendment, is incorrect: it was not proposed until the 20th century (1923, and it never passed).

option_explanations.A: The Equal Rights Amendment was a 20th-century proposal (1923, revived in the 1970s) — not what Anthony's 1876-era movement sought.
option_explanations.B: Anthony's first-wave feminist movement, from Seneca Falls (1848) onward, campaigned above all for women's suffrage — 'universal suffrage' including women.
option_explanations.C: States' rights was the Southern doctrine, not Susan B. Anthony's cause.
option_explanations.D: Prohibition was a parallel reform movement, not the demand of Anthony's excerpt.

items.stem: The excerpts above best support which of the following conclusions?

Women invested with the rights of citizens in one section—voters, jurors, office-holders—crossing an imaginary line, are subjects in the next. In case of divorce on account of adultery in the husband, the innocent wife is held to possess no right to children or property, unless by special decree of the court. But in no State of the Union has the wife the right to her own person, or to any part of the joint earnings of the co-partnership during the life of her husband. In some States women may enter the law schools and practice in the courts; in others they are forbidden. In some universities girls enjoy equal educational advantages with boys, while many of the proudest institutions in the land deny them admittance, though the sons of China, Japan and Africa are welcomed there. But the privileges already granted in the several States are by no means secure.” Source: Susan B. Anthony, “Declaration of Rights for Women,” July 4, 1876
options: The Second Great Awakening, along with various social reform movements, secured full rights for women by the turn of the 19th century.
Before 1876, American women had no right to own property or vote in national elections.
Women’s rights movements flourished despite inconsistent legislation and unequal distributions of power throughout the nation.
American feminists in the 19th century largely focused on suffrage, shunning other social issues such as abolition and prison reform.
items.explanation: Susan B. Anthony’s quote clearly shows that women’s rights varied wildly by state of residence. Choice (B) is too extreme. Choice (A) is likewise too extreme because women did not have “full rights” until the 1970s. Choice (D) is untrue because many first-wave feminists did champion other causes, such as abolition and prohibition.

option_explanations.A: Too extreme: women did not have 'full rights' by 1800 — or even by 1900.
option_explanations.B: Too extreme: the excerpts themselves show some women voting and holding office in certain states, and property rights varied — 'no right' overstates it.
option_explanations.C: Anthony's account of women as voters in one state and 'subjects' in the next shows a patchwork of inconsistent laws — yet the women's-rights movement flourished and grew despite it.
option_explanations.D: Untrue: many 19th-century feminists also championed abolition, temperance, and other reforms alongside suffrage.

items.stem: The above excerpts most closely support which of the following inferences?
items.stimulus: Source 1 “The violent tendencies of dangerous cults can be classified into two general categories—defensive violence and offensive violence. Defensive violence is utilized by cults to defend a compound or enclave that was created specifically to eliminate most contact with the dominant culture. The 1993 clash in Waco, Texas at the Branch Davidian complex is an illustration of such defensive violence. History has shown that groups that seek to withdraw from the dominant culture seldom act on their beliefs that the endtime has come unless provoked.” Source: “Project Megiddo,” U.S. Department of Justice, 2000 Source 2 “Madam Attorney General, I am extremely disappointed in the decisions that have been made out of the Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. In Philadelphia, we had a mayor that bombed people out of an eviction. In Jonestown, we lost the life of my colleague, Congressman Ryan,…because of a miscalculation about cult people. We had Patty Hearst and the Symbionese Liberation Army. We had Wounded Knee with the Indians. Now, when in God’s name is the law enforcement at the Federal level going to understand that these are very sensitive events that you cannot put barbed wire, guns, FBI, Secret Service around them, send in sound 24 hours a day and night and then wonder why they do something unstable? The root cause of this problem was that it was considered a military operation, and it wasn’t. This is a profound disgrace to law enforcement in the United States of America, and you did the right thing by offering to resign….” Source: U.S. Representative John Conyers, Events Surrounding the Branch Davidian Cult Standoff in Waco, Texas: Hearing Before the Committee on the Judiciary, House of Representatives, 1993
options: In the 1990s, antigovernment sentiment, in response to excessive uses of federal power to resolve domestic conflicts, inspired dangerous cults such as the Branch Davidians.
In 1993, Attorney General Janet Reno launched an offensive against the Branch Davidian cult, later drawing criticism from Congress for her heavy-handed approach.
Fearing the offensive violence perpetrated by the Branch Davidian cult, Attorney General Janet Reno sent troops to quell the subsequent standoff and later faced congressional criticism.
Attorney General Janet Reno resigned from office in part because of congressional pressure put on President Clinton by Representative John Conyers.
items.explanation: A careful reading of the excerpts can help you to use POE. There is no evidence that the Branch Davidians were “antigovernment,” (A). According to the first excerpt, they were employing “defensive” measures in response to perceived threats by the federal government, not “offensive” tactics. This likewise rules out (C). Choice (D) is tempting, but notice that Conyers says the Attorney General “offered” to resign. It does not say that she did. (In fact, she did not.)

option_explanations.A: The excerpts do not show antigovernment sentiment inspiring the Branch Davidians. The Justice Department report describes an isolationist group using defensive violence when it felt threatened — not a movement born of antigovernment ideology.
option_explanations.B: The second excerpt (Conyers) criticizes the decisions of Attorney General Janet Reno, the DOJ, and the FBI at Waco. The excerpts support the claim that Reno launched the 1993 operation against the Branch Davidians and drew congressional criticism for a heavy-handed approach.
option_explanations.C: The Justice Department report classifies the Waco violence as defensive, not offensive. Reno did not act out of fear of Branch Davidian offensive violence.
option_explanations.D: Conyers says Reno 'offered' to resign; the excerpt does not say she did resign — and in fact she did not.

options: a violent cult
a federal misuse of power
the site of a bombing
a recent conflict between federal agents and the Lakota people
items.explanation: It helps if you remember that the Wounded Knee incident occurred in 1890, a heavy-handed assault by the U.S. Army against the Lakota people. Choice (A) is incorrect: the Lakota are a Native American tribe, not a cult. There was no bombing, so rule out (C), and Wounded Knee was not a recent conflict, so rule out (D).

option_explanations.A: The Lakota are a Native American nation, not a cult.
option_explanations.B: Wounded Knee (1890) was the U.S. Army's massacre of Lakota people — Conyers invokes it as the archetype of federal misuse of power, paralleling his criticism of the federal assault at Waco.
option_explanations.C: There was no bombing at Wounded Knee; it was an Army assault with rifles and Hotchkiss guns.
option_explanations.D: Wounded Knee (1890) was not recent and was not a standoff between federal agents and the Lakota — it was a massacre by the Seventh Cavalry.
